knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex–Concave Saddle-Point Problem and Primal–Dual Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the saddle problem, saddle points, and the induced primal and dual optimization problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\subset E_x\) and \(\mathcal Y\subset E_y\) be nonempty closed convex sets, and let \(\phi:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, convex in \(x\), and concave in \(y\). Define \(\bar\phi(x)=\sup_{y\in\mathcal Y}\phi(x,y)\), \(\underline\phi(y)=\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\phi(x,y)\), \(\operatorname{Opt}(P)=\min_{x\in\mathcal X}\bar\phi(x)\), and \(\operatorname{Opt}(D)=\max_{y\in\mathcal Y}\underline\phi(y)\). A pair \((x_*,y_*)\) is a saddle point if \(\phi(x,y_*)\geq\phi(x_*,y_*)\geq\phi(x_*,y)\) for all \((x,y)\in\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\). Saddle points exist if and only if \((P)\) and \((D)\) attain equal optimal values. When they exist, the saddle points are exactly the pairs of primal and dual optimal solutions, and \(\phi(x_*,y_*)=\operatorname{Opt}(P)=\inf_x\sup_y\phi(x,y)=\sup_y\inf_x\phi(x,y)=\operatorname{Opt}(D)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous convex–concave function on nonempty closed convex sets, a saddle point satisfies the two-sided saddle inequality. Saddle points exist exactly when the induced primal and dual problems attain the same value, and their optimal-solution pairs are precisely the saddle points.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\subset E_x\) and \(\mathcal Y\subset E_y\) are nonempty closed convex sets.
\(\phi\) is continuous on \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\), convex in \(x\), and concave in \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Saddle}(\phi)\neq\varnothing\iff (P),(D)\text{ are solvable and }\operatorname{Opt}(P)=\operatorname{Opt}(D)\), with saddle points exactly the primal–dual optimal pairs.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Convex–Concave Saddles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional differentiable convex–concave saddle model with a Lipschitz first-order operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty closed convex sets. A function \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) defines a smooth convex–concave saddle problem if \(L(\cdot,y)\) is convex and differentiable on \(X\) for every \(y\in Y\), \(L(x,\cdot)\) is concave and differentiable on \(Y\) for every \(x\in X\), and the saddle operator \(F(x,y)=(\nabla_xL(x,y),-\nabla_yL(x,y))\) is Lipschitz continuous on \(X\times Y\). A saddle point is a pair \((x^\star,y^\star)\) satisfying \(L(x^\star,y)\leq L(x^\star,y^\star)\leq L(x,y^\star)\) for all \((x,y)\in X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth convex–concave saddle has convex and concave differentiable sections, a Lipschitz saddle-gradient operator, and a point satisfying the global two-sided saddle inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) are nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) is finite-valued and continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=(\nabla_xL,-\nabla_yL)\) is the Lipschitz saddle operator, and \((x^\star,y^\star)\) is a saddle exactly when the stated two-sided inequality holds.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Convex–Concave Saddles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex–concave model permitting nondifferentiable sections and set-valued saddle operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty closed convex sets. A proper function \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty,-\infty\}\) defines a nonsmooth convex–concave saddle problem when each section \(L(\cdot,y)\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex, while each section \(L(x,\cdot)\) is proper, upper-semicontinuous, and concave; differentiability is not required. Its saddle operator is the set-valued mapping \(T(x,y)=\partial_xL(x,y)\times\bigl(-\partial_y^+L(x,y)\bigr)\). A pair \((x^\star,y^\star)\) is a saddle point when \(L(x^\star,y)\leq L(x^\star,y^\star)\leq L(x,y^\star)\) for every \((x,y)\in X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsmooth convex–concave saddle permits nondifferentiable convex and concave sections; partial subgradients form a set-valued saddle operator, while solutions obey the two-sided saddle inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty closed convex subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
The relevant convex and concave sections of \(L\) are proper and semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(x,y)=\partial_xL(x,y)\times(-\partial_y^+L(x,y))\) represents the nonsmooth saddle operator.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Convex–Concave Saddles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth coupling plus proximable convex and concave-side nonsmooth terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty closed convex sets. A composite convex–concave saddle problem has the form \[\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}\;\Phi(x,y):=f(x)+K(x,y)-g(y),\] where \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(g:Y\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions, and \(K\) is differentiable, convex in \(x\), and concave in \(y\). Its composite saddle inclusion is \[0\in\bigl(\partial f(x)+\nabla_xK(x,y)+N_X(x),\;\partial g(y)-\nabla_yK(x,y)+N_Y(y)\bigr).\] The model is proximable when the resolvents of the nonsmooth primal and dual terms can be evaluated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composite saddle separates a smooth convex–concave coupling from nonsmooth convex primal and dual terms, yielding a sum of subdifferential, gradient, and normal-cone operators.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
\(K\) is differentiable, convex in its first variable, and concave in its second.
The required proximal mappings of the nonsmooth terms are computable when proximability is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Saddle points are characterized by the displayed composite monotone inclusion.

notation.meaning: normal-cone mappings of the feasible sets

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lagrangian Saddle Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a saddle point of a constrained problem's Lagrangian, with nonnegative inequality multipliers and unrestricted equality multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\phi(x,u,v)=f(x)+u^Tg(x)+v^Th(x)\), a triple \((\bar x,\bar u,\bar v)\) is a Lagrangian saddle point if \(\bar x\in X\), \(\bar u\ge0\), and \[\phi(\bar x,u,v)\le\phi(\bar x,\bar u,\bar v)\le\phi(x,\bar u,\bar v)\] for every \(x\in X\) and every \((u,v)\) with \(u\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lagrangian saddle point maximizes the Lagrangian over admissible dual variables at the fixed primal point and minimizes it over the primal set at the fixed multipliers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in X\ \forall(u,v)\text{ with }u\ge0:\ \phi(\bar x,u,v)\le\phi(\bar x,\bar u,\bar v)\le\phi(x,\bar u,\bar v).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Saddle-Point Characterization and Zero Duality Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes Lagrangian saddle points by fixed-multiplier minimization, primal feasibility, and complementary slackness, and relates them to attained primal and dual optima of equal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi(x,u,v)=f(x)+u^Tg(x)+v^Th(x)\), with \(\bar x\in X\) and \(\bar u\ge0\). Then \((\bar x,\bar u,\bar v)\) is a saddle point if and only if \[\bar x\in\arg\min_{x\in X}\phi(x,\bar u,\bar v),\qquad g(\bar x)\le0,\qquad h(\bar x)=0,\qquad \bar u^Tg(\bar x)=0.\] Moreover, it is a saddle point if and only if \(\bar x\) and \((\bar u,\bar v)\) are respectively optimal for the primal and dual problems and \(f(\bar x)=\theta(\bar u,\bar v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A triple is a Lagrangian saddle point exactly when the primal component minimizes the fixed-multiplier Lagrangian, is feasible, and satisfies complementary slackness. Equivalently, its primal and dual components are attained optima with equal objective values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\bar x,\bar u,\bar v)\text{ is a saddle point}\iff\begin{cases}\bar x\in\arg\min_{x\in X}\phi(x,\bar u,\bar v),\\g(\bar x)\le0,\ h(\bar x)=0,\\\bar u^Tg(\bar x)=0,\end{cases}\iff\bar x,(\bar u,\bar v)\text{ are primal-dual optimal and }f(\bar x)=\theta(\bar u,\bar v).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and convex, let \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be linear, and let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\). For the problem \(\min\{f(x):x\in X,\ Ax=b\}\), the equality-constrained Lagrangian is \(L(x,y)=f(x)+\langle y,Ax-b\rangle\), with unrestricted multiplier \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\). A pair \((x^\star,y^\star)\) is a Lagrangian saddle when \[L(x^\star,y)\leq L(x^\star,y^\star)\leq L(x,y^\star)\quad\text{for all }(x,y)\in X\times\mathbb{R}^m.\] The left inequality forces \(Ax^\star=b\), and the right inequality is equivalent to \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}L(x,y^\star)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine equality constraint with a specified right-hand side is paired with an unrestricted multiplier. A Lagrangian saddle is feasible and minimizes the Lagrangian in the primal variable.
knowledge_statements.title: Equality-Constrained Lagrangian Saddles

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and convex, and let \(g_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Consider minimizing \(f(x)\) over \(x\in X\) subject to \(g_i(x)\leq0\) for every \(i\). The Lagrangian is \(L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i g_i(x)\), with \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\). A pair \((x^\star,\lambda^\star)\in X\times\mathbb{R}_+^m\) is an inequality-constrained Lagrangian saddle if \[L(x^\star,\lambda)\leq L(x^\star,\lambda^\star)\leq L(x,\lambda^\star)\quad\text{for all }(x,\lambda)\in X\times\mathbb{R}_+^m.\] Every such pair satisfies primal feasibility and complementary slackness \(\lambda_i^\star g_i(x^\star)=0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-valued convex inequality constraints use nonnegative multipliers. Any Lagrangian saddle is primal and dual feasible, satisfies complementary slackness, and minimizes the Lagrangian in the primal variable at its selected multiplier.
knowledge_statements.title: Inequality-Constrained Lagrangian Saddles

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Lagrangian Saddles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cone-valued convex constraints paired with multipliers from the dual cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, with dual cone \(K^*=\{y:\langle y,k\rangle\geq0\ \text{for all }k\in K\}\). Consider minimizing a convex function \(f\) over a convex set \(X\) subject to \(G(x)\in-K\), where \(G\) is \(K\)-convex. The conic Lagrangian is \(L(x,y)=f(x)+\langle y,G(x)\rangle\) for \(y\in K^*\). A conic Lagrangian saddle is a pair \((x^\star,y^\star)\in X\times K^*\) satisfying \[L(x^\star,y)\leq L(x^\star,y^\star)\leq L(x,y^\star)\quad\text{for all }(x,y)\in X\times K^*.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone-valued constraint is paired with a dual-cone multiplier; a conic saddle obeys the Lagrangian saddle inequality over primal points and dual-cone multipliers.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
\(X\) is convex, \(f\) is convex, and \(G\) is \(K\)-convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conic constraint \(G(x)\in-K\) induces the multiplier domain \(K^*\) and the displayed saddle formulation.

notation.meaning: dual cone of the constraint cone

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-to-Cone Representation Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation of scalar equalities and inequalities into one product-cone constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(h:X	o\mathbb{R}^p\) encode equality constraints and \(g:X	o\mathbb{R}^q\) encode componentwise inequalities. Define \(G(x)=(h(x),g(x))\) and \(K=\{0\}^p	imes\mathbb{R}_+^q\). Then \[h(x)=0\ 	ext{and}\ g(x)\leq0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G(x)\in-K.\] The dual cone is \(K^*=\mathbb{R}^p	imes\mathbb{R}_+^q\), so a dual vector \(y=(
u,\lambda)\in K^*\) consists of unrestricted equality multipliers \(
u\) and nonnegative inequality multipliers \(\lambda\). Moreover, \[f(x)+\langle y,G(x)angle=f(x)+\langle
u,h(x)angle+\langle\lambda,g(x)angle,\] which is exactly the scalar-constraint Lagrangian.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equalities and componentwise inequalities combine into a product-cone constraint whose dual cone reproduces unrestricted equality multipliers and nonnegative inequality multipliers.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization of the pointwise maximum of finitely many real-valued convex functions on an ambient Euclidean space.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\geq1\), let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, and let \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Define \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(F(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x)\), and consider \[\min_{x\in X}F(x).\] Then \(F\) is convex. For \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=F(x)\}\). If every \(f_i\) with \(i\in I(x)\) is differentiable at \(x\), then \[\partial F(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{\nabla f_i(x):i\in I(x)\}.\] Thus \(F\) may be nondifferentiable where multiple components are active.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-max model optimizes the maximum of finitely many component functions. Convex components yield a convex ambient objective, and at points where active components are differentiable its subdifferential is the convex hull of their gradients.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Max Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\geq1\), let \(a_1,ldots,a_m\in\mathbb{R}\), and define \(\Delta_m=\{y\in\mathbb{R}_+^m:\sum_{i=1}^m y_i=1\}\). Then \[\max_{1\leq i\leq m}a_i=\max_{y\in\Delta_m}\sum_{i=1}^m y_i a_i.\] Consequently, if \(X\) is nonempty and \(f_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), then \[\inf_{x\in X}\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x)=\inf_{x\in X}\max_{y\in\Delta_m}\sum_{i=1}^m y_i f_i(x).\] For each fixed \(x\in X\), every maximizing \(y\in\Delta_m\) is supported on \(I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=\max_{1\leq j\leq m}f_j(x)\}\), and an extreme point \(e_i\) is maximizing whenever \(i\in I(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum of finitely many real values equals maximization of their convex combinations over the simplex. Applying this identity pointwise gives equal outer infima, and maximizing weights are supported on active components.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\geq1\), let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let every \(f_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous and convex. Define \(\Delta_m=\{y\in\mathbb{R}_+^m:\sum_{i=1}^m y_i=1\}\) and \(L(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^m y_i f_i(x)\) on \(X\times\Delta_m\). Then \(L\) is convex in \(x\), linear in \(y\), and \[\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in\Delta_m}L(x,y)=\max_{y\in\Delta_m}\min_{x\in X}L(x,y).\] A pair \((x^\star,y^\star)\in X\times\Delta_m\) is a saddle point if and only if \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x)\), \(y_i^\star=0\) for every \(i\notin I(x^\star)\), where \(I(x^\star)=\{i:f_i(x^\star)=\max_j f_j(x^\star)\}\), and \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\sum_{i=1}^m y_i^\star f_i(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For continuous convex components on a compact convex set, the simplex lift has equal minimax values. Its saddle pairs are exactly finite-max minimizers paired with active-component weights for which the same primal point minimizes the weighted component sum.

children.title: Robust Optimization Saddle Models
children.top_down_role: Saddle formulations driven by deterministic uncertainty sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Robust Optimization Saddle Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case optimization over a deterministic uncertainty set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty decision set, let \(U\) be a nonempty uncertainty set, and let \(\ell:X\times U\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\). A robust optimization saddle model is \[\min_{x\in X}\sup_{u\in U}\ell(x,u).\] When \(X\) and \(U\) are convex, \(\ell(\cdot,u)\) is convex for every \(u\), and \(\ell(x,\cdot)\) is concave for every \(x\), this is a convex–concave saddle problem. A pair \((x^\star,u^\star)\) is a robust saddle if \[\ell(x^\star,u)\leq\ell(x^\star,u^\star)\leq\ell(x,u^\star)\quad\text{for all }(x,u)\in X\times U.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Robust optimization minimizes worst-case loss over a deterministic uncertainty set; convex–concave structure turns the model into a saddle problem.
assumptions_latex: For the saddle classification, \(X,U\) are convex and \(\ell\) is convex–concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The robust worst-case model is \(\min_{x\in X}\sup_{u\in U}\ell(x,u)\), with saddle solutions satisfying the displayed inequalities.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deterministic worst-case model and conditional convex-concave classification are plausible and do not assert saddle existence, but the record supplies no citation. An authoritative robust-optimization source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Distributionally Robust Saddle Models
children.top_down_role: Saddle formulations driven by ambiguity over probability distributions.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributionally Robust Saddle Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case expected-loss optimization over an ambiguity set of probability distributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty decision set, let \(\Xi\) be a measurable sample space, let \(\mathcal{P}\) be a nonempty set of probability measures on \(\Xi\), and let \(\ell:X\times\Xi\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be measurable in its second argument. A distributionally robust saddle model is \[\min_{x\in X}\sup_{P\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim P}[\ell(x,\xi)].\] If \(X\) and \(\mathcal{P}\) are convex, the expected loss is convex in \(x\), and its dependence on \(P\) is affine, then the model is convex–concave. A saddle pair \((x^\star,P^\star)\) satisfies the corresponding two-sided inequality over \(X\times\mathcal{P}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distributionally robust optimization minimizes expected loss under the worst probability law in an ambiguity set; affine dependence on the law supplies the concave side.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{P}\) is a nonempty ambiguity set of probability measures on \(\Xi\).
The expectation exists as an extended real number for every feasible pair.
For the convex–concave classification, \(X,\mathcal{P}\) are convex and the expected loss is convex in \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The adversarial variable is a probability measure \(P\in\mathcal{P}\), and the payoff is \(\mathbb{E}_{P}[\ell(x,\xi)]\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The worst-case expected-loss formulation is standard, but no source is supplied for the ambiguity-set model or for the extended-real measurability and integrability conventions. Those conventions affect whether the payoff and two-sided saddle inequality are well defined, so a located authoritative source is required.

children.title: Uncertainty-Set Representation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits of transferring between pointwise uncertainty and distributional ambiguity.

knowledge_statements.title: Uncertainty-Set Representation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary conditions for representing robust objectives as convex–concave saddle problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(U\) be nonempty sets and let \(\Phi:X\times U\to\mathbb{R}\). If \(U\) is compact and \(u\mapsto\Phi(x,u)\) is upper semicontinuous for every \(x\in X\), then for every \(x\in X\) the supremum \(\sup_{u\in U}\Phi(x,u)\) is attained. If, in addition, \(X\) and \(U\) are convex, \(x\mapsto\Phi(x,u)\) is convex for every \(u\in U\), and \(u\mapsto\Phi(x,u)\) is concave for every \(x\in X\), then \(\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{u\in U}\Phi(x,u)\) has the structure of a convex–concave saddle model. Without compactness or another condition ensuring attainment, the inner supremum may fail to be attained; without concavity in \(u\), methods requiring convex–concave structure do not directly apply.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compactness and upper semicontinuity suffice to attain each inner robust maximum, while convex feasible sets and convex–concave dependence give the standard saddle structure. If attainment or concavity conditions fail, the corresponding representation or algorithmic guarantees may fail.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated conditions respectively provide attainment of the inner supremum and convex–concave saddle structure; their absence can invalidate those properties.

knowledge_statements.title: Nested Minimax Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-depth deterministic nested minimax models with an ordered sequence of optimization operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\geq1\), let \(X_0,\ldots,X_m\) be nonempty sets, let \(f:X_0\times\cdots\times X_m\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), and let \(Q_i\in\{\inf,\sup\}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Define \(V_m(x_0,\ldots,x_{m-1})=Q_m{}_{x_m\in X_m}f(x_0,\ldots,x_m)\) and, recursively, \(V_i(x_0,\ldots,x_{i-1})=Q_i{}_{x_i\in X_i}V_{i+1}(x_0,\ldots,x_i)\) for \(i=m-1,\ldots,1\). The ordered problem \(\inf_{x_0\in X_0}V_1(x_0)\) is a nested minimax model when the sequence contains both infimum and supremum operators, commonly in alternating order. Exchanging adjacent \(\inf\) and \(\sup\) operators is not part of the definition and requires separate interchange conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nested minimax model applies an ordered finite sequence containing minimization and maximization operators to several variable blocks. Changing that order is not generally valid.
assumptions_latex: The displayed extended-real infima and suprema are defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x_0\in X_0}Q_1{}_{x_1\in X_1}\cdots Q_m{}_{x_m\in X_m}f(x_0,\ldots,x_m)\) defines the ordered nested model.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuous and Finite-Sampled Parametric Minimax Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a parametric minimax problem and its finite sampled version without asserting convexity, smoothness, attainment, or approximation guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbf{x}\) be a vector decision variable and let the real-valued parameter \(w\) range over \(\mathcal S\). For an objective \(f(\mathbf{x},w)\), the continuous parametric minimax problem is \(\min_{\mathbf{x}}\max_{w\in\mathcal S}f(\mathbf{x},w)\). Given sampled values \(\mathcal S_d=\{w_i:i=1,\ldots,L\}\subset\mathcal S\), the corresponding discrete minimax problem is \(\min_{\mathbf{x}}\max_{w_i\in\mathcal S_d}f(\mathbf{x},w_i)=\min_{\mathbf{x}}\max_{1\le i\le L}f(\mathbf{x},w_i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parametric minimax problem chooses a vector x to minimize the maximum of f(x,w) over w in S. Replacing S by finitely many sampled parameter values gives the discrete problem of minimizing the largest sampled value.
assumptions_latex: w\in\mathcal S\text{ is a real-valued parameter}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{\mathbf{x}}\max_{w\in\mathcal S}f(\mathbf{x},w),\qquad \min_{\mathbf{x}}\max_{1\le i\le L}f(\mathbf{x},w_i)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the classical variational inequality on a nonempty closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n. The problem \operatorname{VI}(X,f) is to find x^*\in X such that (x-x^*)^{\mathsf T}f(x^*)\geq 0 for every x\in X.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a nonempty closed convex set X and a mapping f from R^n to R^n, VI(X,f) asks for a point x* in X such that the inner product of x−x* with f(x*) is nonnegative for every x in X.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Find }x^*\in X\text{ such that }(x-x^*)^{\mathsf T}f(x^*)\geq0\quad\forall x\in X.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Variational Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine variational inequality on a closed convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), and let \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\). The affine variational inequality \(\operatorname{AVI}(K,M,q)\) is the problem of finding \(x^\star\in K\) such that \[\langle Mx^\star+q,\,y-x^\star\rangle\geq 0\qquad\text{for every }y\in K.\] Equivalently, using the convex-analytic normal cone, \(x^\star\) solves the inclusion \(0\in Mx^\star+q+N_K(x^\star)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine VI seeks a feasible point whose affine field has a nonnegative inner product with every feasible displacement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in K\) solves \(\operatorname{AVI}(K,M,q)\) exactly when \(\langle Mx^\star+q,y-x^\star\rangle\geq0\) for all \(y\in K\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone affine variational inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine variational inequality over a bounded closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $\mathbb E$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let $B(w)=Bw+c:\mathbb E\to\mathbb E^*$ be affine with
\[
\langle Bh,h\rangle\ge0\qquad\forall h\in\mathbb E,
\]
and let $Q\subseteq\mathbb E$ be bounded, closed, and convex. The problem $\operatorname{VI}(Q,B)$ is to find $w^*\in Q$ such that
\[
\langle B(w^*),w-w^*\rangle\ge0\qquad\forall w\in Q.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone affine variational inequality asks for a point in a bounded closed convex set whose affine operator value has a nonnegative pairing with every feasible displacement from that point.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{VI}(Q,B):\ \text{find }w^*\in Q\text{ such that }\langle B(w^*),w-w^*\rangle\ge0\ \forall w\in Q

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Variational Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-dimensional VI with a monotone single-valued operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex and let \(F:K\to\mathbb{R}^n\). The operator \(F\) is monotone on \(K\) when \[\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\geq0\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in K.\] The associated monotone variational inequality is to find \(x^\star\in K\) satisfying \[\langle F(x^\star),y-x^\star\rangle\geq0\qquad\text{for all }y\in K.\] In normal-cone form, its solution condition is \(0\in F(x^\star)+N_K(x^\star)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone VI combines a monotone field with the requirement that its value at the solution form a nonnegative angle with every feasible displacement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F)\) is monotone when \(\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\geq0\) for every \(x,y\in K\).

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudomonotone Variational Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical VI using the standard implication definition of pseudomonotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex and let \(F:K\to\mathbb{R}^n\). The operator \(F\) is pseudomonotone on \(K\) when, for every \(x,y\in K\), \[\langle F(x),y-x\rangle\geq0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\langle F(y),y-x\rangle\geq0.\] A pseudomonotone variational inequality is the problem of finding \(x^\star\in K\) such that \(\langle F(x^\star),y-x^\star\rangle\geq0\) for every \(y\in K\), under this operator property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pseudomonotone VI uses an operator whose nonnegative directional pairing at one point implies the corresponding nonnegative pairing at the comparison point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is pseudomonotone precisely when the displayed implication holds for all \(x,y\in K\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed implication is a standard finite-dimensional pseudomonotonicity definition, but no source is supplied. An authoritative locator is required because several pseudomonotonicity notions occur in the literature.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmonotone Variational Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical VI whose operator violates monotonicity on the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex and let \(F:K\to\mathbb{R}^n\). The variational inequality seeks \(x^\star\in K\) satisfying \[\langle F(x^\star),y-x^\star\rangle\geq0\qquad\text{for all }y\in K.\] It is nonmonotone on \(K\) when monotonicity fails, equivalently when there exist \(x,y\in K\) such that \(\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle<0\). This classification alone supplies neither existence nor uniqueness of a solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonmonotone VI has the usual variational inequality condition but its field violates the monotonicity inequality for at least one feasible pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The VI is nonmonotone exactly when \(\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle<0\) for some \(x,y\in K\).

knowledge_statements.title: Expectation Variational Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-stage stochastic VI defined by an expected operator on a deterministic feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})\) be a probability space, let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(G:K\times\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be measurable in its random argument with \(G(x,\cdot)\) integrable for every \(x\in K\). Define \(F(x)=\mathbb{E}[G(x,\omega)]\). The expectation variational inequality is to find \(x^\star\in K\) such that \[\langle \mathbb{E}[G(x^\star,\omega)],y-x^\star\rangle\geq0\qquad\text{for every }y\in K.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expectation VI replaces a random field by its mean and imposes the ordinary VI condition on that expected field.
assumptions_latex: \(G(x,\cdot)\) is measurable and integrable for every \(x\in K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(K,\mathbb{E}[G(\cdot,\omega)])\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The expected-operator formulation is mathematically plausible and internally consistent, but no authoritative source or locator supports the selected stochastic-VI formulation and its integrability assumptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Sample-Average Variational Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical finite-sample approximation of a single-stage expectation VI.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the expectation-VI setting, let \(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_N\) be independent samples with law \(\mathbb{P}\), and define the sample-average operator \[F_N(x)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}G(x,\omega_i).\] The sample-average variational inequality is the random finite problem of finding \(x_N\in K\) such that \[\langle F_N(x_N),y-x_N\rangle\geq0\qquad\text{for every }y\in K.\] Thus the expectation operator \(F(x)=\mathbb{E}[G(x,\omega)]\) is represented computationally by its empirical average \(F_N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sample-average VI replaces the expected random operator by the arithmetic mean of finitely many sampled realizations and solves the resulting deterministic VI.
assumptions_latex: \(G(x,\omega_i)\) is finite for every \(x\in K\) and sampled outcome.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F_N)\) is the sample-average representation of \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The empirical-operator representation is plausible and the representation content kind fits, but the record has no source supporting this definition or its sampling assumptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Random-Set Variational Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measurable-selection formulation with outcome-dependent feasible sets and operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})\) be a probability space, let \(K:\Omega\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) be a measurable random closed convex set with nonempty values, and let \(G:\mathbb{R}^n\times\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be jointly measurable on the graph of \(K\). A pathwise random-set variational inequality seeks a measurable selection \(x^\star:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \(x^\star(\omega)\in K(\omega)\) and \[\langle G(x^\star(\omega),\omega),y-x^\star(\omega)\rangle\geq0\quad\text{for every }y\in K(\omega)\] for \(\mathbb{P}\)-almost every \(\omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random-set VI seeks a measurable decision that solves an outcome-wise VI on the feasible set realized in each outcome.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a measurable, nonempty-valued, closed convex random set.
\(G\) is measurable on the graph of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star(\omega)\in\operatorname{SOL}(K(\omega),G(\cdot,\omega))\) for \(\mathbb{P}\)-almost every \(\omega\).

notation.meaning: solution set of a variational inequality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Random-set VIs have multiple inequivalent formulations. No source establishes that this leaf should use the pathwise measurable-selection formulation or that the stated measurability assumptions suffice for the intended model.

knowledge_statements.title: Multistage Variational Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space VI over square-integrable policies adapted to a finite filtration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})\) carry a filtration \((\mathcal{F}_t)_{t=0}^{T}\). Let \(\mathcal{H}=\prod_{t=0}^{T}L^2(\Omega,\mathcal{F}_t,\mathbb{P};\mathbb{R}^{n_t})\), let \(K\subseteq\mathcal{H}\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(F:K\to\mathcal{H}\). A multistage variational inequality seeks an adapted policy \(x^\star\in K\) such that \[\sum_{t=0}^{T}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\langle F_t(x^\star),y_t-x_t^\star\rangle\right]\geq0\qquad\text{for every }y\in K.\] The filtration enforces that each stage decision uses only information available by that stage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multistage VI is a Hilbert-space VI over adapted policies, with feasibility and operator interactions coupled across decision stages.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\) satisfies the VI in the adapted-policy Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}\).

notation.meaning: Hilbert space of square-integrable adapted policies

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The adapted-policy Hilbert-space VI is plausible, but multistage VIs admit several formulations. An authoritative source is needed to validate this formulation, its policy space, and the stage-component operator assumptions.

children.title: Nonanticipative Information Structure
children.top_down_role: Stagewise information restrictions governing admissible multistage solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonanticipative Information Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measurability condition preventing a staged decision from using future information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})\) carry a filtration \(\mathcal{F}_0\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\mathcal{F}_T\). A stochastic policy \(x=(x_0,\ldots,x_T)\) is nonanticipative when each component \(x_t:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{n_t}\) is \(\mathcal{F}_t\)-measurable. Equivalently, whenever two outcomes are indistinguishable using information in \(\mathcal{F}_t\), their stage-\(t\) decisions agree up to null-set modifications. For square-integrable policies, the nonanticipative policy space is \[\mathcal{N}=\prod_{t=0}^{T}L^2(\Omega,\mathcal{F}_t,\mathbb{P};\mathbb{R}^{n_t}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonanticipativity requires each stage decision to depend only on information revealed by that stage, never on future observations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is nonanticipative if and only if \(x_t\) is \(\mathcal{F}_t\)-measurable for every \(t\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Adaptedness via stagewise measurability is standard, but no source is supplied. The additional pointwise claim about outcomes being indistinguishable is not automatically well-defined on an arbitrary probability space and requires a precise information-partition formulation or omission.

children.title: Generalized Variational Models
children.top_down_role: Extensions whose state-dependent constraints or additional bifunction structure change available theory.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Variational Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mixed VI combining a single-valued field with a convex extended-real function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(F:K\to\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(\varphi:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex with \(K\cap\operatorname{dom}\varphi\neq\varnothing\). The mixed variational inequality is to find \(x^\star\in K\cap\operatorname{dom}\varphi\) such that \[\langle F(x^\star),y-x^\star\rangle+\varphi(y)-\varphi(x^\star)\geq0\qquad\text{for every }y\in K.\] If \(\delta_K\) denotes the convex indicator of \(K\), this condition is equivalently \(0\in F(x^\star)+\partial(\varphi+\delta_K)(x^\star)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed VI augments the ordinary VI pairing by the change in a convex function; equivalently, it adds the subdifferential of that function together with the feasible-set indicator to the operator inclusion.
assumptions_latex: \(\varphi:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\) solves the mixed VI exactly when the displayed inequality holds for every \(y\in K\), equivalently when \(0\in F(x^\star)+\partial(\varphi+\delta_K)(x^\star)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Quasivariational Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space quasivariational inequality with a solution-dependent feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(D\subseteq H\), let \(K:D\rightrightarrows D\) have nonempty values, and let \(F:D\to H\). The quasivariational inequality associated with \((F,K)\) is the problem of finding \(x^\star\in D\) such that
\[
x^\star\in K(x^\star)\quad\text{and}\quad \langle F(x^\star),y-x^\star\rangle\ge 0\quad\text{for every }y\in K(x^\star).
\]
When \(K(x)=C\) for every \(x\in D\), where \(C\subseteq D\) is fixed, this reduces to the Stampacchia variational inequality on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasivariational inequality is a variational inequality whose feasible set depends on the unknown solution itself.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(D\subseteq H\).
\(K(x)\subseteq D\) is nonempty for every \(x\in D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in K(x^\star)\) and \(\langle F(x^\star),y-x^\star\rangle\ge0\) for all \(y\in K(x^\star)\).

notation.meaning: Feasible set associated with the candidate point x.

knowledge_statements.title: Equilibrium Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard bifunction equilibrium problem on a prescribed feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty subset of a real vector space and let \(g:C\times C\to\mathbb{R}\) be a bifunction satisfying the normalization \(g(x,x)=0\) for every \(x\in C\). The equilibrium problem for \(g\) is to find \(x^\star\in C\) such that
\[
g(x^\star,y)\ge 0\quad\text{for every }y\in C.
\]
For an inner-product space and \(g(x,y)=\langle F(x),y-x\rangle\), this predicate is precisely the Stampacchia variational inequality for \(F\) on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An equilibrium solution is a feasible point whose bifunction value against every feasible comparison point is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in C\) and \(g(x^\star,y)\ge0\) for every \(y\in C\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bifunction formulation is standard, internally consistent, and appropriate as a definition of an equilibrium problem. No source or specific locator is supplied, so its evidence requirement is unmet.

children.title: Global Saddle Solutions

knowledge_statements.title: Global Saddle Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global saddle point for a two-player minimization-maximization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be nonempty sets and let \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\). A pair \((x^\star,y^\star)\in X\times Y\) is a global saddle solution of \(L\) if
\[
L(x^\star,y)\le L(x^\star,y^\star)\le L(x,y^\star)
\quad\text{for every }(x,y)\in X\times Y.
\]
Thus \(x^\star\) globally minimizes \(L(\cdot,y^\star)\), while \(y^\star\) globally maximizes \(L(x^\star,\cdot)\). The definition does not itself require convexity, concavity, differentiability, compactness, or existence of any other saddle pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global saddle solution simultaneously minimizes the payoff in the first variable and maximizes it in the second variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(x^\star,y)\le L(x^\star,y^\star)\le L(x,y^\star)\) for all \((x,y)\in X\times Y\).

children.title: Global Minimax Solutions
children.top_down_role: Global solution concepts stated through nested minimizing and maximizing values.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Minimax Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal and dual global minimax optimizers, allowing a nonzero duality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be nonempty sets and let \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\). Define
\[
p(x)=\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y),\qquad d(y)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y).
\]
A pair \((x^\star,y^\star)\in X\times Y\) is a global minimax solution pair when
\[
x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}p(x)
\quad\text{and}\quad
y^\star\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in Y}d(y).
\]
This definition does not require equality between the primal value \(\inf_{x\in X}p(x)\) and the dual value \(\sup_{y\in Y}d(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global minimax pair consists of a primal worst-case minimizer and a dual best guaranteed-value maximizer, possibly separated by a duality gap.
assumptions_latex: The displayed argmin and argmax sets are nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\) and \(y^\star\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Saddle–Minimax Correspondence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence under attainment and zero minimax gap; convex-concave compact problems form a standard sufficient regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\), and suppose \(x^\star\) minimizes \(p(x)=\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\), \(y^\star\) maximizes \(d(y)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)\), and
\[
\inf_{x\in X}p(x)=\sup_{y\in Y}d(y)\in\mathbb{R}.
\]
Then \((x^\star,y^\star)\) is a global saddle solution. Conversely, every global saddle solution yields both minimax optimizers and equality of these values. In particular, attainment and equality hold when \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty compact convex subsets of finite-dimensional spaces and \(L\) is continuous, convex in \(x\), and concave in \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Attained primal and dual minimax solutions form a saddle pair exactly when their values coincide; continuous compact convex-concave problems satisfy this regime.
assumptions_latex: \(x^\star\) and \(y^\star\) attain the primal and dual minimax values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(x^\star,y)\le L(x^\star,y^\star)\le L(x,y^\star)\) for all \((x,y)\in X\times Y\).

children.title: Stampacchia VI Solutions
children.top_down_role: Variational-inequality solutions organized around evaluation at the candidate point.

knowledge_statements.title: Stampacchia VI Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-valued Stampacchia variational inequality in a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subseteq H\) be nonempty, and let \(F:C\to H\). A point \(x^\star\in C\) is a Stampacchia variational-inequality solution for \((F,C)\) if
\[
\langle F(x^\star),y-x^\star\rangle\ge 0
\quad\text{for every }y\in C.
\]
Equivalently, when \(C\) is closed and convex, it satisfies the normal-cone inclusion \(0\in F(x^\star)+N_C(x^\star)\), with \(N_C(x^\star)=\{v\in H:\langle v,y-x^\star\rangle\le0\text{ for all }y\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Stampacchia solution evaluates the operator at the unknown point and requires a nonnegative inner product toward every feasible comparison point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in C\) and \(\langle F(x^\star),y-x^\star\rangle\ge0\) for every \(y\in C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Minty VI Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-valued Minty variational inequality in a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subseteq H\) be nonempty, and let \(F:C\to H\). A point \(x^\star\in C\) is a Minty variational-inequality solution for \((F,C)\) if
\[
\langle F(y),y-x^\star\rangle\ge 0
\quad\text{for every }y\in C.
\]
Unlike the Stampacchia predicate, the operator is evaluated at each comparison point \(y\). The definition is meaningful without monotonicity, although equivalence with the Stampacchia solution set requires additional hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Minty solution tests the operator at every feasible comparison point and requires its direction away from the candidate to be nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in C\) and \(\langle F(y),y-x^\star\rangle\ge0\) for every \(y\in C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subseteq H\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(F:C\to H\) be monotone:
\[
\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\ge 0\quad\text{for all }x,y\in C.
\]
Every Stampacchia solution is then a Minty solution. If, additionally, \(F\) is hemicontinuous along feasible segments, meaning that \(t\mapsto\langle F(x+t(y-x)),y-x\rangle\) is continuous at \(t=0^+\) for all \(x,y\in C\), every Minty solution is a Stampacchia solution. Hence, under both hypotheses, the two solution sets coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Monotonicity sends Stampacchia solutions to Minty solutions; feasible-segment hemicontinuity supplies the reverse implication, so both solution sets coincide.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Minimax Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential local minimax notion for smooth or nonsmooth finite-dimensional games.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\). A pair \((x^\star,y^\star)\) is a local minimax solution if there exist \(\delta_0>0\) and a function \(h:(0,\delta_0]\to(0,\infty)\), with \(h(\delta)\to0\) as \(\delta\downarrow0\), such that for every \(0<\delta\le\delta_0\),
\[
L(x^\star,y)\le L(x^\star,y^\star)\le
\max_{\|y'-y^\star\|\le h(\delta)}L(x,y')
\]
whenever \(\|x-x^\star\|\le\delta\) and \(\|y-y^\star\|\le\delta\). The maximizing player may therefore react locally to the minimizing player's perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local minimax point locally maximizes in the second variable and locally minimizes the resulting response value under a shrinking reaction neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: The displayed local maxima exist for sufficiently small \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^\star,y^\star)\) satisfies the displayed shrinking-neighborhood minimax inequalities.

notation.meaning: Radius allowed for the maximizing player's local response.
Radius of the minimizing player's perturbation neighborhood.

children.title: Game-Stationary Points
children.top_down_role: First-order stationary notions associated with strategic game variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Game-Stationary Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order stationary point of a differentiable constrained zero-sum game.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty closed convex sets, and let \(L\) be continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(X\times Y\). A pair \((x^\star,y^\star)\in X\times Y\) is game-stationary if
\[
\langle\nabla_xL(x^\star,y^\star),x-x^\star\rangle\ge0
\quad\text{and}\quad
\langle-\nabla_yL(x^\star,y^\star),y-y^\star\rangle\ge0
\]
for every \(x\in X\) and \(y\in Y\). For interior points, this reduces to \(\nabla_xL(x^\star,y^\star)=0\) and \(\nabla_yL(x^\star,y^\star)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A game-stationary point satisfies the first-order minimization condition in the first variable and maximization condition in the second.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty closed convex subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^\star,y^\star)\) satisfies both displayed first-order variational inequalities.
review_flags: The supplied stationary-point locator does not explicitly cover constrained zero-sum game stationarity.

children.title: Local-Solution Correspondence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where stationarity does or does not support a local minimax interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Local-Solution Correspondence Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth quadratic separation between local minimax, game stationarity, and local saddle behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(L(x,y)=-x^2+4xy-y^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\). The point \((0,0)\) is game-stationary. It is also a local minimax solution: for \(|x|\le\delta\), choosing \(h(\delta)=2\delta\) gives
\[
\max_{|y|\le h(\delta)}L(x,y)=3x^2\ge L(0,0)=0,
\]
and \(L(0,y)=-y^2\le0\). Nevertheless, \((0,0)\) is not a local saddle point because \(L(x,0)=-x^2<0=L(0,0)\) for every nonzero \(x\). Thus local minimax and stationarity need not imply the local saddle inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth quadratic game has a stationary local minimax point that is not a local saddle point, separating these solution concepts.
assumptions_latex: Local minimax is interpreted by the shrinking-response definition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((0,0)\) is game-stationary and local minimax but is not a local saddle point.

notation.meaning: Local response radius establishing the minimax predicate.

review_flags: Constructed counterexample requires independent source support or reviewer validation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quadratic calculations are internally correct: the point is stationary, satisfies the stated shrinking-response local-minimax predicate, and fails the local saddle inequality. The counterexample content kind fits the boundary leaf, but it has no source or explicit standard-field rationale and depends on an unsourced local-minimax definition.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty closed convex sets, and let \(L\) be real-valued and differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(X\times Y\). Suppose that \(L(\cdot,y)\) is convex on \(X\) for every \(y\in Y\) and that \(L(x,\cdot)\) is concave on \(Y\) for every \(x\in X\). Set \(Z=X\times Y\) and define
\[
F(x,y)=\bigl(\nabla_xL(x,y),-\nabla_yL(x,y)\bigr).
\]
Then \(z^\star=(x^\star,y^\star)\in Z\) is a global saddle solution if and only if
\[
\langle F(z^\star),z-z^\star\rangle\ge 0\quad\text{for every }z\in Z.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
0\in F(z^\star)+N_Z(z^\star),
\]
where \(N_Z\) is the convex-analytic normal cone to \(Z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable convex-concave saddle point is exactly a solution of the variational inequality generated by the gradient in the minimizing variable and the negative gradient in the maximizing variable.

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Inclusion Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between a variational inequality and a normal-cone inclusion on a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subset H\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(F:C\to H\). Define \(N_C(x)=\{v\in H:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le 0\ \text{for every }y\in C\}\) for \(x\in C\). Then \(x^\star\in C\) solves the variational inequality \(\langle F(x^\star),y-x^\star\rangle\ge 0\) for every \(y\in C\) if and only if \[0\in F(x^\star)+N_C(x^\star).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point solves the variational inequality exactly when the negative operator value belongs to the set’s normal cone there.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in \operatorname{VI}(C,F)\iff 0\in F(x^\star)+N_C(x^\star)\).

notation.meaning: Convex-analytic normal cone to C at x.
Solution set of the variational inequality induced by F on C.

knowledge_statements.title: Projected Fixed-Point Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection fixed-point form of a Hilbert-space variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subset H\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(F:C\to H\), and fix \(\gamma>0\). A point \(x^\star\in C\) satisfies \(\langle F(x^\star),y-x^\star\rangle\ge 0\) for every \(y\in C\) if and only if \[x^\star=P_C\bigl(x^\star-\gamma F(x^\star)\bigr),\] where \(P_C\) is the metric projection onto \(C\). The equivalence holds for every positive \(\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variational-inequality solution is precisely a fixed point of a projected forward step of any positive length.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\iff x^\star=P_C(x^\star-\gamma F(x^\star))\).

knowledge_statements.title: Integrable VI Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variational inequalities generated by gradients of differentiable convex potentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(\Phi\) be differentiable and convex on an open set containing \(C\). For the integrable operator \(F=\nabla\Phi\), a point \(x^\star\in C\) satisfies \[\langle F(x^\star),x-x^\star\rangle\ge 0\quad\text{for every }x\in C\] if and only if \[x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\Phi(x).\] Thus the variational inequality generated by a convex potential represents its constrained minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variational inequality whose operator is a convex potential’s gradient has exactly the potential’s constrained minimizers as solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi\) is differentiable and convex on an open neighborhood of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\Phi(x)\).

notation.meaning: Gradient operator generated by the potential.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The gradient-VI/minimization equivalence is standard and precisely stated, but the record supplies no citation or inspectable locator.

children.title: Convex Optimization Representations

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Optimization Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order inclusion and variational-inequality representations of constrained convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subset H\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Then \[x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in\partial f(x^\star)+N_C(x^\star),\] provided the subdifferential sum rule applies at \(x^\star\). If \(f\) is differentiable near \(C\), this is equivalently \(\langle\nabla f(x^\star),x-x^\star\rangle\ge0\) for every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constrained convex minimizers are zeros of the objective subdifferential plus the constraint normal cone, or solutions of the gradient VI when differentiable.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
A qualification ensuring \(\partial(f+\delta_C)=\partial f+N_C\) holds at the candidate point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{C}f\iff0\in\partial f(x^\star)+N_C(x^\star)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Potential–Operator Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional criterion and path-integral construction for a gradient potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and simply connected, and let \(F:U	o\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable. There exists \(\Phi\in C^2(U)\) with \(F=
abla\Phi\) if and only if the Jacobian is symmetric everywhere: \[
abla F(x)=
abla F(x)^{\mathsf T}\quad	ext{for every }x\in U.\] For a fixed \(x_0\in U\), the potential is determined up to an additive constant by \[\Phi(x)-\Phi(x_0)=\int_{\gamma_{x_0,x}}\langle F(u),duangle,\] where the integral is independent of the piecewise smooth path \(\gamma_{x_0,x}\subset U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a simply connected domain, a continuously differentiable operator is a gradient exactly when its Jacobian is symmetric; path integration recovers the potential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(F=
abla\Phi\) for some \(\Phi\in C^2(U)\iff
abla F(x)=
abla F(x)^{\mathsf T}\) for all \(x\in U\).

notation.meaning: Piecewise smooth path from the base point to x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional integrability criterion and path-integral construction are standard under the stated hypotheses, but no source or locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: KKT-System Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex differentiable program represented by its primal–dual KKT system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(\min_x f(x)\) subject to \(g_i(x)\le0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\) and \(Ax=b\), where \(f,g_i:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}\) are differentiable and convex and the affine constraints satisfy Slater's condition. A triple \((x^\star,\lambda^\star,
u^\star)\) is primal–dual optimal if and only if it satisfies \[
abla f(x^\star)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i^\star
abla g_i(x^\star)+A^{\mathsf T}
u^\star=0,\] \[g(x^\star)\le0,\quad Ax^\star=b,\quad\lambda^\star\ge0,\quad\lambda_i^\star g_i(x^\star)=0\ 	ext{for all }i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under convexity and Slater’s condition, primal–dual optimal solutions are exactly the triples satisfying stationarity, feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementary slackness.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and every \(g_i\) are differentiable and convex.
A Slater point satisfies \(g_i(x)<0\) for all \(i\) and \(Ax=b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^\star,\lambda^\star,\nu^\star)\) is primal–dual optimal if and only if it satisfies the displayed KKT system.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The convex KKT equivalence is standard under Slater's condition, but it has no citation. A sourced version should also explicitly introduce the dimensions of A and b.

knowledge_statements.title: Nash Variational-Inequality Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variational-inequality representation of a differentiable convex game on a product strategy set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\) players choose \(x_i\in X_i\subset\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\), where each \(X_i\) is nonempty, closed, and convex. Suppose each cost \(J_i(x_i,x_{-i})\) is differentiable and convex in \(x_i\) for every fixed \(x_{-i}\). Set \(X=\prod_iX_i\) and \(F(x)=\operatorname{col}(\nabla_{x_i}J_i(x))_{i=1}^N\). Then \(x^\star\in X\) is a Nash equilibrium if and only if \[\langle F(x^\star),x-x^\star\rangle\ge0\quad\text{for every }x\in X.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a differentiable game with convex individual problems, Nash equilibria are exactly solutions of the VI formed from players’ partial gradients.
assumptions_latex: Each strategy set \(X_i\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
Each \(J_i(\cdot,x_{-i})\) is differentiable and convex on \(X_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\) is a Nash equilibrium if and only if \(x^\star\in\operatorname{VI}(X,F)\).

notation.meaning: Strategy profile of all players except player i.
Game pseudo-gradient formed from players’ partial gradients.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Nash-equilibrium VI representation is mathematically standard for fixed product strategy sets and playerwise convex differentiable costs, but no citation or locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complementarity representation of the multivalued signum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the scalar multivalued signum graph through two complementarity pairs and an auxiliary scalar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a,\widehat a\in\mathbb{R}\), where \(\operatorname{sgn}(a)=1\) if \(a>0\), \(\operatorname{sgn}(0)=[-1,1]\), and \(\operatorname{sgn}(a)=-1\) if \(a<0\), one has \(\widehat a\in\operatorname{sgn}(a)\) if and only if there exists \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(0\le 1+\widehat a\perp -a+\lambda\ge0\) and \(0\le\lambda\perp1-\widehat a\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar belongs to the multivalued signum of a exactly when an auxiliary scalar exists satisfying the two stated complementarity conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat a\in\operatorname{sgn}(a)\iff\exists\lambda\in\mathbb{R}:\ 0\le1+\widehat a\perp-a+\lambda\ge0,\quad 0\le\lambda\perp1-\widehat a\ge0.

knowledge_statements.title: Complementarity Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonlinear complementarity representation of a variational inequality on the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}_+^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\). A point \(x^\star\in\mathbb{R}_+^n\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(\mathbb{R}_+^n,F)\) if and only if it solves the nonlinear complementarity problem \[x^\star\ge0,\qquad F(x^\star)\ge0,\qquad \langle x^\star,F(x^\star)\rangle=0.\] Equivalently, the componentwise relations \(x_i^\star F_i(x^\star)=0\) hold for every \(i=1,\ldots,n\), together with nonnegativity of both complementary vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A VI on the nonnegative orthant is equivalent to nonnegativity of the point and operator value together with componentwise complementarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in\operatorname{VI}(\mathbb{R}_+^n,F)\iff 0\le x^\star\perp F(x^\star)\ge0\).

notation.meaning: The vectors have zero inner product.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The orthant VI and nonlinear-complementarity equivalence is correct, but the record has no supporting source or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Map Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-map equation equivalent to a variational inequality over a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^n\), and fix \(\gamma>0\). Define the normal map by \[F^{\mathrm{nor}}_\gamma(z)=\gamma F(P_Cz)+z-P_Cz.\] If \(F^{\mathrm{nor}}_\gamma(z^\star)=0\), then \(x^\star=P_Cz^\star\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\), and \(z^\star=x^\star-\gamma F(x^\star)\). Conversely, if \(x^\star\in\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\), then \(z^\star=x^\star-\gamma F(x^\star)\) satisfies \(P_Cz^\star=x^\star\) and \(F^{\mathrm{nor}}_\gamma(z^\star)=0\). Thus \[\{P_Cz:F^{\mathrm{nor}}_\gamma(z)=0\}=\operatorname{VI}(C,F).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting any zero of the normal map gives a variational-inequality solution, and every such solution has the normal-map zero obtained by subtracting its scaled operator value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{P_Cz:F^{\mathrm{nor}}_\gamma(z)=0\}=\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\), with \(z=x-\gamma F(x)\) for each corresponding solution \(x\).

notation.meaning: Scaled normal map associated with F and C.

knowledge_statements.title: NCP-Function Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equation representation of complementarity using the Fischer–Burmeister NCP function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the Fischer–Burmeister function by \(\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(a,b)=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}-a-b\). For real \(a,b\), \[\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(a,b)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a\ge0,\ b\ge0,\ ab=0.\] Hence, for \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(\Phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^n\) componentwise by \((\Phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x))_i=\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x_i,F_i(x))\). Then \[\Phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\le x\perp F(x)\ge0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying the Fischer–Burmeister function componentwise converts a nonlinear complementarity problem into an equivalent system of nonsmooth equations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x)=0\iff0\le x\perp F(x)\ge0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Fischer–Burmeister equivalence and componentwise equation representation are correct, but no authoritative citation or locator is supplied.

children.title: Primal–Dual Value Relations
children.top_down_role: Value correspondences linking primal, dual, saddle, and variational formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Value Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak and saddle-point strong duality for a convex–concave Lagrangian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be nonempty sets and let \(L:X\times Y\to[-\infty,+\infty]\). Define \[p^\star=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y),\qquad d^\star=\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y).\] Weak duality always gives \(d^\star\le p^\star\). If \((x^\star,y^\star)\) is a saddle point, meaning \(L(x^\star,y)\le L(x^\star,y^\star)\le L(x,y^\star)\) for all \((x,y)\in X\times Y\), then \[d^\star=p^\star=L(x^\star,y^\star),\] and both outer extrema are attained at \(y^\star\) and \(x^\star\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual value never exceeds the primal value; a saddle point makes them equal to its Lagrangian value and attains both.
assumptions_latex: The displayed infima and suprema are interpreted in the extended-real sense.
For the equality conclusion, \((x^\star,y^\star)\) satisfies the saddle inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^\star\le p^\star\), and a saddle point implies \(d^\star=p^\star=L(x^\star,y^\star)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Duality-Gap Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal–dual gap as a nonnegative saddle-point residual and optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be nonempty and let \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\). For \((x,y)\in X\times Y\), define the primal–dual gap \[G(x,y)=\sup_{v\in Y}L(x,v)-\inf_{u\in X}L(u,y),\] whenever both terms are finite. Then \(G(x,y)\ge0\). Moreover, \(G(x,y)=0\) if and only if \[L(x,v)\le L(x,y)\le L(u,y)\quad\text{for every }u\in X,v\in Y,\] so zero gap is equivalent to \((x,y)\) being a saddle point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal–dual gap is nonnegative, and—when finite—it vanishes exactly at saddle points, providing a directly checkable optimality residual.
assumptions_latex: The supremum and infimum defining \(G(x,y)\) are finite at the evaluated pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G(x,y)\ge0\), and \(G(x,y)=0\iff(x,y)\) is a saddle point of \(L\) on \(X\times Y\).

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Operator Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued monotonicity on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\). The operator \(A\) is monotone when
\[
\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq 0
\]
for every \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\). The monotone operator regime consists of inclusion problems \(0\in A x\) for which this inequality is available, without assuming maximality, strong monotonicity, single-valuedness, or continuity of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator is monotone when every pair of graph points has a nonnegative primal–dual displacement pairing; no maximality or quantitative modulus is assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq0\) for all \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\).

notation.meaning: A possibly set-valued operator on the Hilbert space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone operator

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An operator \(M:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is monotone if, for every \(x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[\left\langle M(x_2)-M(x_1),x_2-x_1\right\rangle\ge 0.\]

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}^n,\quad \left\langle M(x_2)-M(x_1),x_2-x_1\right\rangle\ge 0

knowledge_statements.title: Maximally Monotone Operator Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-maximal monotonicity on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be monotone. The operator \(A\) is maximally monotone if no monotone operator \(B:H\rightrightarrows H\) has \(\operatorname{gra}A\subsetneq\operatorname{gra}B\). Equivalently, whenever \((x,u)\in H\times H\) satisfies \(\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq0\) for every \((y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\), one has \(u\in Ax\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone operator is maximally monotone when its graph admits no proper monotone enlargement, equivalently every point monotonically related to its graph already belongs to it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is maximally monotone exactly when every point monotonically related to \(\operatorname{gra}A\) lies in \(\operatorname{gra}A\).

notation.meaning: The graph of the set-valued operator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone and maximal monotone operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for a possibly set-valued operator on finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An operator T:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n is monotone if \langle u-v,x-y\rangle\ge 0 for all (x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{Gra}T. A monotone operator T is maximal monotone if no monotone operator S satisfies \operatorname{Gra}T\subsetneq\operatorname{Gra}S.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A possibly set-valued operator is monotone when every two pairs in its graph satisfy the monotonicity inequality. It is maximal monotone when its graph has no proper monotone extension. In the equivalent set-valued expression, the inequality is vacuous if an argument is outside the operator's domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is monotone}\iff (\forall (x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{Gra}T)\;\langle u-v,x-y\rangle\ge0;\qquad T\text{ is maximal monotone}\iff T\text{ is monotone and }\nexists S\text{ monotone with }\operatorname{Gra}T\subsetneq\operatorname{Gra}S.

children.title: Maximality Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Consequences and limitations associated with the presence or absence of maximality.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximality Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minty surjectivity separates maximal monotonicity from mere monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be monotone, and let \(\lambda>0\). Then \(A\) is maximally monotone if and only if
\[
\operatorname{ran}(I+\lambda A)=H.
\]
Thus failure of maximality is witnessed by some \(z\in H\) for which \(z\notin x+\lambda Ax\) for every \(x\in H\); at such a point the resolvent \((I+\lambda A)^{-1}\) is not defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone operator crosses the maximality boundary exactly when its shifted range fills the space; otherwise its resolvent is undefined at some point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is maximally monotone if and only if \(\operatorname{ran}(I+\lambda A)=H\).

notation.meaning: The resolvent associated with \(A\) and parameter \(\lambda\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Operator extensions and maximal monotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines graph extensions and maximal monotonicity and records the full-domain resolvent consequence in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For operators \(\mathbb A,\overline{\mathbb A}:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\), \(\overline{\mathbb A}\) is an extension of \(\mathbb A\) if \(\operatorname{Gra}\overline{\mathbb A}\supseteq\operatorname{Gra}\mathbb A\), and a proper extension if this inclusion is strict. A monotone operator is maximal monotone if it has no proper monotone extension. If \(\mathbb A\) is maximal monotone, then \(\operatorname{dom}\mathbb J_{\mathbb A}=\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extension contains the original operator's graph and is proper when that containment is strict. A monotone operator is maximal monotone when it has no proper monotone extension. In finite-dimensional Euclidean space, the resolvent of a maximal monotone operator has full domain.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb A\text{ is monotone for the maximality definition}
\mathbb A\text{ is maximal monotone for the resolvent-domain conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dom}\mathbb J_{\mathbb A}=\mathbb R^n

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full-domain continuous monotone operators are maximal monotone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The source defines continuity for an operator to include full domain and single-valuedness; the final boundary statement is not a converse characterization of maximality.

If such an operator is monotone, then it is maximal monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Here a continuous operator is full-domain, single-valued, and continuous as a function. Every such monotone operator is maximal monotone. Thus nontrivial maximality questions arise outside this class, notably for discontinuous or set-valued operators.

children.title: Strongly Monotone Operator Regime
children.top_down_role: Operator geometry governed by a fixed strong-monotonicity modulus.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Monotone Operator Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic monotonicity modulus on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\). For \(\mu>0\), the operator \(A\) is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone if
\[
\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq \mu\lVert x-y\rVert^2
\]
for all \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\). The strongly monotone regime assumes that at least one such positive modulus \(\mu\) is known or exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong monotonicity strengthens monotonicity by lower-bounding the graph pairing with a positive quadratic function of the input separation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq\mu\lVert x-y\rVert^2\) for all graph pairs.

children.title: Uniformly Monotone Operator Regime
children.top_down_role: Operator geometry governed by a general uniform growth modulus.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniformly Monotone Operator Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive distance-dependent monotonicity modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\). The operator \(A\) is uniformly monotone if there exists an increasing function \(\phi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty]\) satisfying \(\phi(0)=0\) and \(\phi(t)>0\) for every \(t>0\), such that
\[
\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq\phi(\lVert x-y\rVert)
\]
for every \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform monotonicity supplies a strictly positive lower bound, depending only on input distance, for the pairing of any two distinct graph points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq\phi(\lVert x-y\rVert)\) for all graph pairs.

children.title: Monotonicity-Modulus Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions induced by linear, nonlinear, or local monotonicity moduli.

knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity-Modulus Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unified representation of quantitative monotonicity classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\). A monotonicity-modulus regime is represented by a function \(\omega:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty]\) with \(\omega(0)=0\) through
\[
\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq\omega(\lVert x-y\rVert)
\]
for all \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\). Ordinary monotonicity corresponds to \(\omega\equiv0\); uniform monotonicity requires \(\omega(t)>0\) for \(t>0\); and \(\mu\)-strong monotonicity corresponds to \(\omega(t)=\mu t^2\) with \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single distance modulus organizes ordinary, uniform, and strong monotonicity by changing the lower bound imposed on graph-point pairings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The choices \(\omega\equiv0\), \(\omega(t)>0\) for \(t>0\), and \(\omega(t)=\mu t^2\) encode monotone, uniformly monotone, and strongly monotone regimes, respectively.

knowledge_statements.title: Cocoercive Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-valued inverse-strong monotonicity on a convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(A:C\to H\). For \(\beta>0\), the operator \(A\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive if
\[
\langle Ax-Ay,x-y\rangle\geq\beta\lVert Ax-Ay\rVert^2
\]
for all \(x,y\in C\). In particular, every cocoercive operator is monotone and \(1/\beta\)-Lipschitz continuous on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cocoercivity lower-bounds the input–output pairing by the squared output change; it implies both monotonicity and a reciprocal Lipschitz bound.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle Ax-Ay,x-y\rangle\geq\beta\lVert Ax-Ay\rVert^2\) for all \(x,y\in C\).
